title: US charges three in $129M AI voice-cloning CEO fraud scheme
subtitle: A Southern District of New York indictment alleges the trio cloned executive and lawyer voices to trick accounting staff worldwide into wiring funds to overseas accounts.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Federal prosecutors in Manhattan unsealed an indictment this week charging Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit with running a $129 million AI-powered impersonation ring. The scheme used voice — and in some cases video — clones of real chief executives and outside attorneys to call corporate accounting staff and order wire transfers to accounts controlled by the defendants. Victims included a Missouri hospital system that lost roughly $4.83 million, a California hospital system that lost about $2.97 million, and a Rhode Island bank that lost about $2.68 million. The defendants face conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, two counts of aggravated identity theft, money laundering conspiracy, and two money laundering counts.

The indictment is one of the largest AI-impersonation fraud cases to date and the first to break out the mechanics in detail. Prosecutors say the group spent months collecting audio samples of each target executive — earnings call recordings, keynote clips, podcast appearances — before generating cloned voices with commercial AI tools. The call script followed a predictable two-step: the fake CEO introduced an urgent deal, then an impersonated lawyer followed up with wire instructions. Several victims reported the voice was indistinguishable from the real executive, and in at least one case the fraudsters also joined a video conference with a synthesized face.

The case lands as AI-enabled business email compromise shifts from proof-of-concept to a repeatable playbook. Industry breach reports through 2026 have tracked a steady rise in voice-cloning fraud, but most prior cases involved single victims or isolated incidents. A coordinated multi-victim indictment with named defendants, bank accounts, and victim totals changes the picture — it establishes a prosecutable fact pattern that other districts can now use as a template. The timing also pressures banks and enterprise finance teams to adopt callback verification policies that treat a familiar voice as insufficient on its own.

A note for learners: identity verification built for the pre-AI era assumed a voice or face was a credential. It no longer is. If you are building any workflow that authorizes a payment, a password reset, or a privileged action — even informally inside a small team — assume an attacker can produce a convincing synthesized version of any public-facing executive. The practical defense is procedural: a known callback number, an out-of-band confirmation channel, or a shared secret that was never spoken on a recording. Technical detection of synthetic audio helps at the margin, but process is what actually stops the wire from leaving.
